title: Seeing Me in the Arms of Death, Phyllis
text:
Seeing me in the arms of death, Phyllis

heroically was moved to clemency,

and gave her proud decorum leave

to bend down and remedy my fate.


The subject felt, by a power stronger

than the natural, the sweet violence;

for love in the crucible of experience

turns accidents into health.


If they no longer fled, Phyllis, from the glory

that there they saw come forth from your beauty,

which in its presence is all light and life;


nature remained astonished,

helped against its own laws,

and love prided itself on the victory.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the paradox of love curing death by violating nature's own laws.

title: Now It Shines in Me as Native
text:
Now it shines in me as native,

Laura, your candor, not as alien;

for it serenely calms my indomitable affection,

generous and alive in its errors,


as from bright Pollux is derived

the force that soothes the sea and bridles Eurus,

so that, filled with fraternal honor,

dark Castor may receive it.


By virtue, then, of love so noble and strong,

which, despite natural snares,

turns what is most earthly into celestial,


let us pride ourselves on being celestial lovers;

let the union of two substances, without death,

acknowledge neither time nor fortune.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the Castor-Pollux conceit and the lovers' wish to outrun time.

title: When You Look at Me, Clori, Full of Light
text:
When you look at me, Clori, I imagine

myself a horizon filled with light before your eyes;

your sun acts on the dark affection

as it acts on the serene spirit;


and when from within my breast I try

to return high reflections to the effective light,

what is luminous and pure responds well,

but the earthly exhales its mists.


Then your gaze is not sun, but dawn,

it dispels its imperfect vapor;

but if perhaps it strives to form a cloud,


against itself it shines;

because the moment it rises to your sphere

your noble radiance inflames and gilds it.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the sun/dawn metaphor for a beloved gaze that transforms earthly mist.

title: Loose Your Hair to the Playful Zephyr
text:
Loose your hair to the playful zephyr,

so that it may repay, oh Cynthia, for a while,

some of the many hours the arrangement usurps,

which adds to it not grace, but weight.


How much more light, than crowned or imprisoned,

it reveals to us, waving without reserve!

And tell me whether in the laws of adornment

art ever answered with such great success.


Let ambitious splendors be offered

by waves and the mines of the Orient

to the hair of insecure kings.


Do not curl or gild yours;

and since it grew upon so free a brow,

let it imitate her pride, let it keep no laws.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the argument for natural loose hair over jeweled artifice.

title: I Know Well, Cynthia, the Worship Owed
text:
I know well, Cynthia, the worship owed

to the one who, from two unequal substances,

forms mortals so superior

that each is a god of a brief world;


and that this honor obliges him to rise

above the being of natural works,

and, assaulting those fatal machines,

live joined to the cause that moves them;


and with this I am the one whom your love diverts

from the use of this great knowledge

by the divinity of your beauty;


and it lives so intent on venerating you

that it groans if perhaps it imagines

that its idolatry can have an end.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the philosophical elevation of man interrupted by Cynthia's beauty.

title: I Flee from You, and Arrive at Your Thresholds
text:
I flee from you, and arrive at your thresholds,

faithless like you, Gala, and fear to find you;

sad, for I seek in dangers a part

faithful and safe for my calm.


Your frauds can be that, I do not deny it;

but seeing you, who could disarm you?

My new defenses already wanted art,

and I deliver them to your perfidious whim.


I will die complaining and yours, Gala,

having been an incredible fable

of indiscreet faith and shameful pain.


Oh justice of love! For it is not possible

for me to agree with you though you are good,

nor to stop loving you though you are bad!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the lover's paradox of fleeing to the beloved's dangerous threshold.

title: To a Woman Who Painted Her Face and Was Beautiful
text:
I want to confess to you, Don Juan, first,

that that white and color of Doña Elvira

has nothing of hers, if one looks closely,

except that it cost her money.


But after that I want to confess to you

that the beauty of her lie is so great

that in vain does equal beauty of a true face

aspire to compete with it.


But is it any wonder that I go astray

for such a deception, since we know

that Nature deceives us in this way?


For that blue sky that we all see

is neither sky nor blue. Great pity

that so much beauty is not true!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the witty defense of cosmetics by comparing them to the illusion of the blue sky.

title: These Are the Saguntine Relics
text:
These are the Saguntine relics,

injury and glory to the successor of Belus,

when heaven saw them in an exalted structure

near the source of light for the world.


They lie captive to ivy, and among thorns

with which the frozen ground arms its crags,

and today they release vengeance and consolation

in the contemplation of their ruins.


Saguntum values more being wept

by posterity than if, with favorable fortune,

it had given laws to Carthage.


Oh you, who survive the havoc,

candid faith, see to it that I die,

if love has equal pity kept for me.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the ruin meditation on Saguntum and the turn toward faithful death in love.

title: Love, Who in My Deep Thought
text:
Love, who in my deep thought

has his noble forces readied,

sometimes comes armed up to the eyes,

from where I present them to Cynthia's.


But she, opposed to the rare daring,

so that in future it may be restrained,

withholds that laughter, that favor,

with which she usually relieves suffering.


My sweet lord flees to his center,

fearful and courteous; for there is no subject

that shows courage against her disdain.


I turn aside from the lightning, not because of the effect

it has on mortals,

but because it serves a celestial precept.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the militarized Love retreating before Cynthia's celestial restraint.

title: That Bird, Cynthia, Which from the Ice
text:
That bird, Cynthia, which from the ice

flees to your hands, and with boldness,

when you release it, stubbornly returns,

where did it learn the faith of our zeal?


She guided it to the second flight,

and thus obliged to so jealous a guide,

it will not return to the nest, however much day

clears the air that clouds its sky.


Oh faithful little bird! since you equal us

in that affection you hold so vividly,

if they give you freedom, return to surrender yourself,


return to seek glory in disdain,

for twice Love, to animate you

to so happy a flight, gave you his wings.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the bird as emblem of willingly renewed captivity in love.
